system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 10 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-05-18 00:04:00 to 2179-05-27 09:43:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with low-grade fever, malaise, and increased abdominal distension. He had recently been exposed to a family member with cold symptoms. Workup included negative blood, urine, and ascites cultures, ruling out bacteremia and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Imaging showed stable cirrhosis and new but non-urgent findings in the liver and lung. His symptoms were attributed to a viral upper respiratory infection, which improved with supportive care including fluticasone. A therapeutic paracentesis removed 2 liters of fluid. Nutrition recommended reducing tube feeding duration from 18 to 16 hours daily due to suspected caloric excess. He remained stable on his transplant regimen, including Remodulin for portopulmonary hypertension. He was discharged home with improved symptoms and follow-up planned with his liver team.
problems: Acute upper respiratory infections of unspecified site
Esophageal varices in diseases classified elsewhere, without mention of bleeding
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ was admitted to the surgical service with known 
cirrhosis for which he had been on the transplant list for a 
year.  On ___, he underwent a deceased donor liver 
transplant which was uncomplicated. The reader is referred to 
the operative note for further details.  In the immediate 
post-operative period, he was stable and not requiring any 
pressors.  He was maintained on his home dose of remodulin for 
pulmonary hypertension as well as a nitric oxide gtt in order to 
maintain mean pulmonary artery pressures less than 40mmHg.    He 
subsequent underwent a liver duplex that show patent vasculature 
however with slightly elevated velocities in the main hepatic 
artery.  Liver function test were trended and demonstrated 
decreasing transaminases and bilirubin levels.  On POD1,  he was 
weaned off of the nitric oxide gtt and started on TID sildenafil 
for his pulmonary hypertension, again maintaining low PA 
pressures.  He did desat shortly after however but had a 
negative bronch and shortly recovered on his own.  Tacrolimus 
was started in addition to his already administered 
immunosuppressants including MMF and methylprednisone.  On POD2, 
he was extubated without problem.  He maintained his O2 sats and 
had low PA pressures.  Given his stable PA pressures the 
Swan-ganz catheter was removed.  Drain outputs were noted to be 
high (with serosangiouness) output and as such he was given 
fluid replacement with alubmin (12.5g per 2L of drain output).  
He was subsequently advanced to the liver pathway protocol.  On 
POD4 he was transferred to the floor in stable condition.  
Immunosuppression was continued and changed according to trough 
level measured each morning.  Prophylactic antibiotics were 
administered according to protocol.  The valcyte was reduced in 
the setting of acute renal failure.  Over the next 3 days, he 
was again maintained on the liver transplant pathway. He 
remained hemodynamically stable, afebrile, had downtrending 
LFT's, resolving renal failure, and worked with ___ to regain his 
strength.  Also in the setting and in conjunction with the 
Pulmonary team his remodulin was turned down from 44 to 42ng/kg 
which he seemed to tolerated well. 

On POD8, Mr. ___ was found to be acutely tachycardic and 
tachypneic.  Given the findings, he was transferred to the 
surgical intensive care unit where a full set of labs and a 
liver duplex were obtained.  His transaminases were noted to be 
dramatiacally elevated.  His liver duplex showed a patent but 
stenotic hepatic artery.  There was a slight area of hepatic 
infarct however this was felt not to be contributing to his 
symptoms.  Over the next few hours he continued to decompensate 
and was eventually intubated.  Shortly there after, increasing 
amounts of pressors were required.  The decision was made to 
image using a CT scan which demonstrated gas-formng abscess in 
the liver.  Exploratory laparotomy was performed but no driage 
of the abscess could be performed; necrotic liver was debrided.  
See the OP note for furter details. Into POD9, he increasingly 
had a pressor requirement and maxed out on 4 agents.  He went 
into renal failure and reqired CVVH.  In conjunction with his 
health care proxy the decision was made to no longer pursue 
aggressive measures.  He expired shortly after.  Cultures from 
the exploration revealed E.coli in the liver and his blood cx 
were consistent with an E. coli bacteremia.  

We suspect the liver had been seeded with E Coli prior to 
donation as the donor had a history of IV drug use.

HISTORY:  End-stage renal disease, liver transplant.  Pre-op evaluation.

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior chest radiographs including most recent from ___ and scout image from abdominal/pelvic CT from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  PA and lateral chest radiographs.  

FINDINGS:

An enteric tube courses below the diaphragm, tip is not included on this
examination.  A right central line terminates in the mid to lower SVC.  The
cardiac silhouette is top-normal in size, not significantly changed since
prior examination.  New right lung base opacity likely relates to atelectasis.
There is atelectasis at the left lung base.  No focal consolidation, large
pleural effusion or pneumothorax is identified.  

IMPRESSION:

New opacity in the right lower lobe is likely atelectasis.  No evidence of
pneumonia.

HISTORY:  ___ man status post liver transplant.

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior radiographs the chest dated ___
through ___.

FINDINGS:

Portable semi-upright radiograph of the chest demonstrates atelectasis and
congestion at the bilateral bases.  The heart is top normal in size. 
Endotracheal tube is seen with the tip terminating 5 cm above the carina. 
Swan-Ganz catheter is seen with the tip in the right pulmonary artery.  Right
IJ seen with tip terminating in the cavoatrial junction.  A second right
internal jugular catheter is seen with the tip at the level of the thoracic
inlet.  Nasogastric tube is seen with the tip in the stomach.

HISTORY:  Status post liver transplant, evaluate patency of hepatic artery and
portal vein.

TECHNIQUE:  Liver ultrasound and Doppler.

COMPARISON:  None.

FINDINGS:

Liver Doppler:  The main portal, right portal and left portal vein are patent
with normal hepatopetal flow.  Elevated velocities are seen within the main
portal vein, reaching up to 134 cm/second, which is not unexpected within 24
hours after transplant.  The right, middle and left hepatic veins are patent. 
The main hepatic artery is patent and shows a brisk systolic upstroke.  Given
the increase in end-diastolic velocities, the resistive indices of the right
and left hepatic arteries are 0.42 and 0.38, respectively.  The IVC is patent.

Liver ultrasound:  There is no intrahepatic fluid collection.  There is a

Doppler evaluation demonstrates a patent main, right, and left portal veins

Markedly elevated velocities (150-200+cm/sec) are again noted in the main

raise concern for a portal venous stenosis.

notable in the left lobe.  There is also a focal peripheral area of decreased
echogenicity within the left lobe raising concern for infarct.

2. Persistently elevated main portal vein velocities similar to the previous
exam with notably discrepant lower velocities within the intrahepatic right
and left portal veins.  Findings raise concern for a portal venous stenosis. 
Further evaluation with CTA is recommended given this finding as well as the
gas seen in the liver noted above.

Swan-Ganz catheter terminates in the distal right pulmonary artery, similar to

film.  

2.  ET tube and Swan-Ganz catheter are in unchanged position.  Advancement of
the ET tube by 2-3 cm and withdrawal of the Swan-Ganz catheter by 3-4 cm is

HISTORY:  Status post liver transplant, tachycardia and hypoxia. Assess for
pulmonary embolus as well as questionable wedge infarction on recent
ultrasound.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT axial images were acquired through the chest during the
pulmonary arterial phase of enhancement with 130 mL of Omnipaque. 
Subsequently, a CT of the abdomen and pelvis was performed during the venous
phase of enhancement.  Coronal and sagittal reformations were provided and
reviewed.

DLP:  972 mGy/cm.

COMPARISON:  Liver ultrasound degenerative tear ___.

FINDINGS:

CTA chest:  The timing of contrast limits evaluation for subsegmental
pulmonary emboli.  Within this limitation, there are no large filling defects
to indicate a pulmonary embolus.  An apparent filling defect within the right
upper lobe pulmonary artery is thought to relate to flow artifact or a lymph
node (6:  108).  The aorta and main pulmonary artery are normal in caliber. 
Diffuse enlargement of the peripheral pulmonary arteries may indicate
underlying portal pulmonary syndrome.  

An endotracheal tube is in satisfactory position.  Debris is seen surrounding
the inflated cuff.  The airways are patent through the segmental level. 
Collapse or consolidation are seen within the lower lobes bilaterally.  There
is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax.  A small focus of ground-glass opacity
is seen in the left upper lung (6:76).  

The heart is mildly enlarged.  A Swan Ganz catheter is present, terminating
within the right main pulmonary artery.  A right-sided tunneled hemodialysis
catheter terminates in the right atrium.  There is no supraclavicular,
axillary or or central lymphadenopathy.  

Abdomen:  The patient is status post a liver transplant.  There are 2 large
infarctions involving almost the entirety of the left lobe, the largest
measuring 11.5 x 8.9 cm.  Both collections show internal loculated air and
branching air consistent with pneumobilia.  Hypodensities are also seen
peripherally in the right lobe worrisome for infarction as well.  Fluid fills
the hila and extends into the region of the duodenum.  Periportal
lymphadenopathy is unchanged from prior.  A intermediate common hyperdense 3.5
x 3.3 cm collection displaces the native inferior vena cava laterally and may
indicate an underlying hematoma (8: 17).  An abdominal drain is positioned
posterior to the liver.  

The timing of contrast limits complete evaluation of the hepatic vasculature. 
The portal venous system appears patent however, there is an abrupt transition
in caliber between the extra and intrahepatic main portal vein.  This, in
part, is thought secondary to significant periportal edema.  The known
replaced main hepatic artery is not optimally visualized but presumed patent
given the findings on the same day liver ultrasound.  The superior mesenteric
artery is patent.  The left hepatic vein is diminutive.  Markedly enlarged
splenic varices are present and unchanged.  

The spleen remains markedly enlarged.  Scattered calcifications are consistent
with prior granulomatous disease.  There is a small amount of ascites
scattered throughout the abdomen and pelvis.  The pancreas and adrenal glands
are unremarkable.  

A wedge shaped hypodensity is seen in the posterior right kidney consistent
with infarction (8: 26).  There is no hydronephrosis.  A simple cyst seen in
the upper pole of the right kidney is unchanged.  

The stomach is unremarkable.  An enteric tube terminates within the body of
the stomach.  There is diffuse thickening of small bowel which may relate to
portal congestion.  There is no evidence for obstruction.  The large bowel is
unremarkable.  

Pelvis:  A Foley catheter is present.  The rectum is unremarkable.  There is
no inguinal or pelvic sidewall lymphadenopathy. 

Bones and soft tissues:  Fusion hardware is seen at L5-S1.  Multilevel
compression deformities, worst at T9, are unchanged.  There is anasarca.  

IMPRESSION: 1.  Timing of contrast severely limits the evaluation for
pulmonary embolus, however, there is no large pulmonary embolus seen.  2. 
Infarctions involve almost the entirety of the left lobe and are scattered
peripherally in the right lobe.  Timing of the contrast limits evaluation of
the hepatic vasculature, however, the replaced main hepatic artery is likely
patent given the findings on the same day ultrasound.  3.  Abrupt change in
caliber from the intra to extrahepatic main portal vein.  While this may
indicate stenosis, there is likely an element of mass-effect from significant
periportal edema.  4.  Peripheral infarction in the right kidney.  5.  Diffuse
small bowel thickening may relate to portal congestion.  6.  Bilateral lower
lobe consolidations.  7.  Dilated pulmonary vasculature consistent with portal
pulmonary syndrome.  

These findings were discussed with Dr. ___ by Dr. ___ at 17:18 on ___ 5 min after discovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, we’ve admitted you today because you’re getting your liver transplant. You’ve been on the list for a while, and a donor has become available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, doc. I’m ready. I’ve been waiting for this. How soon will it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The surgery is scheduled for this morning. We’ll take you to the OR around noon. You’ll be under general anesthesia, and the team will replace your liver with the donor’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pulmonary hypertension? I’m still on Remodulin. Will that be okay during surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep your Remodulin running throughout. We’ll also use nitric oxide during the surgery to help keep your pulmonary pressures low and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m nervous, but I trust you. What about recovery after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go to the ICU after. We’ll monitor your new liver closely—check blood flow, liver enzymes, and how you’re tolerating the transplant. You’ll be on a ventilator at first, but we hope to take you off soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just updating you—we’ve completed the liver transplant. It went smoothly. The new liver is in, and blood flow looks good so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your liver this evening. The hepatic artery and portal vein are both open and flowing well. There’s some expected swelling, but nothing concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My breathing feels a bit heavy though. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re still on the ventilator, and we see some atelectasis—collapsed lung areas—on the X-ray. We’re suctioning and adjusting your settings to help expand your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your liver enzymes are starting to come down. That’s a sign the new liver is functioning. We’re also seeing improvement in your chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. When can I breathe on my own?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try to wean you off the ventilator tomorrow. Your pressures are stable, and we’ve started sildenafil to help with your pulmonary hypertension instead of nitric oxide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re off the nitric oxide, and your PA pressures are still under 40. That’s excellent. We’ll keep you on sildenafil three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better already. Any sign of rejection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’re monitoring your tacrolimus levels daily and adjusting your immunosuppressants. So far, no signs of rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been extubated and are breathing on your own. Swan-Ganz catheter has been removed. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. Can I sit up now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll start physical therapy soon. Your drain output is high, so we’re giving albumin to help with fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a new central line today to help with medications and monitoring. Your kidney function is a bit off—we’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the surgery or my old kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely a mix. We’ve reduced Valcyte because it can affect kidneys. We expect it to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are trending well—creatinine is down, liver enzymes continue to improve. You’re moving to the regular floor today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I feel stronger. Any more tests coming up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep doing daily labs. The team is happy with your progress so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still stable. Your Remodulin dose was slightly reduced to 42 ng/kg/min. You’re tolerating it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any reason for the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pulmonary pressures are stable, so we’re cautiously reducing it. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urine culture shows minimal growth—nothing to treat. You remain afebrile and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another liver ultrasound this morning. We’re seeing gas in the liver—especially the left lobe—and some signs of possible infarction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gas? In my liver? That sounds bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is concerning. It could mean an infection or poor blood flow. We’re ordering a CT scan to get a better look.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows multiple infarcts in the left lobe and some in the right. There’s air in the liver, which suggests a gas-forming infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? But I haven’t had a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Immunosuppressants can mask symptoms. We’ve started broad-spectrum antibiotics and are preparing for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate and breathing are increasing. We’re moving you to the ICU.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve intubated you because your oxygen levels dropped. We’re giving pressors to support your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Blood cultures are back. They show E. coli. It’s likely the infection came from the donor liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the transplant… it’s infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It appears so. We’re taking you to surgery to remove the infected tissue and check the blood vessels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Post-op update: we found a large abscess with gas. We couldn’t drain it fully, but we removed necrotic tissue and checked the hepatic artery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the liver still working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unfortunately, the damage is severe. Your liver enzymes are very high, and your kidneys are failing. We’ve started CVVH.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve spoken with your health care proxy. Given how sick you are, we’re shifting to comfort care only.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So… no more fighting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you comfortable. You’re not alone. We’re here with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is dropping despite four pressors. Your organs are shutting down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m tired… just let me go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re with you. You’re safe. We’ll keep you pain-free.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, I’m sorry. Despite everything, your body couldn’t recover. You passed peacefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe the E. coli came from the donor, who had a history of IV drug use. It seeded the liver before transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll inform your family and begin the process of notifying the transplant network about the donor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The cultures from the liver tissue confirmed E. coli, matching the blood results. It was a multi-drug resistant strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re documenting everything for the medical review board. This was an unexpected complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your care team is grieving with your family. You were a strong patient, and we did everything we could.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring for any public health implications due to the resistant E. coli.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The hospital chaplain has spoken with your proxy. They’re arranging next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve completed the post-mortem documentation. Your case will be reviewed to improve future transplant safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, thank you for your courage. You faced this with dignity. We’ll remember you.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for a deceased donor liver transplant due to HCV cirrhosis and decompensated liver disease. The transplant was performed successfully on 2179-05-18, and initial recovery was stable with improving liver function and weaning from nitric oxide to sildenafil for portopulmonary hypertension. By postoperative day 8, he acutely decompensated with tachycardia and respiratory failure. Imaging revealed hepatic infarcts and gas-forming abscesses. Blood and tissue cultures confirmed E. coli bacteremia, likely seeded from the donor liver. Despite surgical debridement and intensive support, he developed multi-organ failure and septic shock. After discussion with his health care proxy, care was transitioned to comfort measures, and he expired on 2179-05-26.
